title: Enterprise Deployment Models
description: On-prem vs. cloud vs. hybrid AI, air-gapped deployments, private model hosting, and a deployment decision framework.

lessons.title: On-Prem vs. Cloud vs. Hybrid AI
lessons.description: The deployment-model decision that shapes almost every other choice in this course.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain the trade-offs between **on-premises**, **cloud**, and **hybrid** deployment for enterprise AI systems.

sections.title: 🏢 On-premises: full control, full responsibility
sections.content:
Running AI infrastructure entirely within an organization's own data centers gives complete control over data location, hardware, and security posture — at the cost of the organization bearing all the operational burden the Cloud course's infrastructure modules covered:

- Procurement
- Maintenance
- Scaling
- Disaster recovery

None of it offloaded to a provider.

sections.title: ☁️ Cloud: less operational burden, less control
sections.content: Using a public cloud provider (the Cloud course's core subject) offloads infrastructure operations to the provider in exchange for real control trade-offs: data residing on infrastructure the organization doesn't own, and dependency on the provider's own security and availability practices — the same **managed-versus-self-hosted** trade-off from the Vector Databases course's choosing-a-database lesson, now at the scale of an entire organization's AI infrastructure.

sections.title: 🤝 Hybrid: splitting the difference deliberately
sections.content: A **hybrid** approach keeps some workloads on-premises (often the most sensitive data or strictly regulated workloads) while running others in the cloud (typically less sensitive, more elastic-capacity-dependent workloads) — not a compromise taken by default, but a deliberate split based on which workload actually needs which model's specific strengths.

sections.title: 🧭 Why enterprises face this decision differently than a startup
sections.content: A regulated enterprise often has legal, contractual, or compliance obligations dictating where certain data can live — obligations a smaller, less regulated organization typically doesn't face — which is exactly why this decision gets its own dedicated course specifically for the enterprise context rather than being fully covered by the general Cloud course.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating hybrid as a default compromise rather than a deliberate split.** Splitting workloads without a clear rule for which goes where recreates the operational complexity of both models without the benefits of either — hybrid only pays off when the split is based on each workload's actual needs.

**Assuming a smaller organization's cloud-vs-on-prem calculus applies unchanged to a regulated enterprise.** As the lesson notes, legal and contractual data-location obligations can force a decision a startup would never have to make on pure cost or convenience grounds.

**Choosing cloud purely for lower perceived operational burden without checking data-control requirements first.** If a contractual or regulatory obligation rules out third-party infrastructure entirely, the operational-convenience argument for cloud is moot before it's even weighed.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off an organization accepts by choosing full on-premises AI infrastructure?
options: Complete control over data and security posture, in exchange for bearing the full operational burden themselves
Zero operational responsibility with complete control simultaneously
Guaranteed lower cost than any cloud alternative in every case
No need for any data security practices at all
questions.explanation: On-premises deployment maximizes control but shifts every operational burden — procurement, maintenance, scaling, DR — onto the organization itself, with no provider to offload it to.

questions.question: Why might a hybrid deployment model be chosen deliberately, rather than as a default compromise?
options: Because different workloads have genuinely different needs — some requiring on-premises control for sensitive data, others benefiting from cloud elasticity
Because hybrid deployment is always cheaper than either pure option
Because hybrid deployment eliminates the need for any security considerations
Because cloud providers do not allow enterprises to use their services at all
questions.explanation: A deliberate hybrid split matches each workload's actual requirements to the deployment model best suited for it, rather than treating hybrid as a lazy middle ground.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `choose_deployment` return "on-premises (or tightly controlled hybrid)" for the patient records assistant regardless of its `ops_capacity`?
options: Because `has_strict_jurisdiction_requirement=True` triggers the function's first `if` branch, which returns immediately without evaluating sensitivity or ops capacity at all
Because patient records always have `data_sensitivity="low"`
Because `ops_capacity="medium"` always maps to on-premises
Because the function ignores the jurisdiction flag entirely
questions.explanation: The function checks `has_strict_jurisdiction_requirement` first and returns immediately if it's `True` — the other parameters are never even reached, mirroring how categorical compliance requirements override other considerations.

questions.question: In the code example, why does the internal analytics dashboard resolve to "cloud"?
options: Because it has `data_sensitivity="low"` and no jurisdiction requirement, matching the `if data_sensitivity == "low"` branch
Because it has the highest `ops_capacity` of all four workloads
Because all workloads default to cloud unless explicitly excluded
Because analytics dashboards are hardcoded as a special case
questions.explanation: With no jurisdiction requirement and `data_sensitivity="low"`, the function skips the first two branches and matches `if data_sensitivity == "low": return "cloud"`.

questions.question: In the code example, what does the trading model inference workload resolve to, and why?
options: "cloud", because `ops_capacity` is low
"hybrid", because it has `data_sensitivity="high"` and `ops_capacity="low"`, matching the second branch, with no jurisdiction requirement to short-circuit earlier
"on-premises (or tightly controlled hybrid)", because of a jurisdiction requirement
It raises an error because no branch matches
questions.explanation: `has_strict_jurisdiction_requirement=False` skips the first branch; `data_sensitivity == "high" and ops_capacity == "low"` matches the second branch, returning the hybrid recommendation.

questions.question: Per the "☁️ Cloud" section, what trade-off does using a public cloud provider involve?
options: Less operational burden in exchange for data residing on infrastructure the organization doesn't own and dependency on the provider's own security and availability practices
No trade-offs at all compared to on-premises deployment
Complete elimination of any security responsibility for the organization
Guaranteed higher cost than on-premises in every scenario
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly frames cloud as trading operational burden for real control trade-offs — the same managed-vs-self-hosted trade-off pattern seen in the Vector Databases course.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating hybrid deployment as a default compromise rather than a deliberate split?
options: Because splitting workloads without a clear rule for which goes where recreates the operational complexity of both models without the benefits of either
Because hybrid deployment is technically impossible to implement in practice
Because hybrid deployment always costs more than either pure on-prem or pure cloud
Because regulators forbid hybrid deployment for any enterprise
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section states this directly: an undisciplined hybrid split loses the clarity benefit of choosing deliberately, ending up with both models' overhead and neither's clean benefits.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against choosing cloud purely for lower operational burden without first checking data-control requirements?
options: Because if a contractual or regulatory obligation rules out third-party infrastructure entirely, the operational-convenience argument for cloud is moot before it's even weighed
Because cloud infrastructure is always more expensive than on-premises regardless of requirements
Because data-control requirements never actually affect deployment choice in practice
Because cloud providers cannot offer any operational convenience benefits
questions.explanation: This mirrors the lesson's core point: categorical compliance obligations can eliminate cloud as an option entirely, making the operational-convenience argument irrelevant if checked too late.

lessons.title: Air-Gapped Deployments
lessons.description: When 'no internet access at all' is a hard requirement, not just a preference.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what an **air-gapped** deployment requires and why it demands different tooling than a typical connected system.

sections.title: 🚫 What air-gapped means
sections.content: An **air-gapped** environment has no network connection to the outside internet at all — common in defense, intelligence, and some highly regulated financial or healthcare contexts where the risk of any external connection is considered unacceptable, regardless of how well-secured that connection might otherwise be.

sections.title: 📦 Why this breaks a lot of standard AI tooling assumptions
sections.content:
Nearly every workflow covered throughout this curriculum assumes internet access at some point:

- Pulling a container image from a registry (Cloud course)
- Calling a hosted LLM API (LLM Engineering course)
- Downloading a model from Hugging Face (Hugging Face course)

An air-gapped deployment needs every one of these dependencies pre-staged and transferred in through an approved, controlled process before the system can run at all.

sections.title: 🔄 Updates become a deliberate, manual process
sections.content: Because there's no live connection to pull updates, patches, or new model versions, an air-gapped system's update process is inherently manual and batched — someone has to vet and physically transfer each update through the approved channel, which is slower and requires real planning ahead compared to a connected system's automatic patching.

sections.title: 🧭 The trade-off this exists for
sections.content: Air-gapping trades operational convenience and update speed for the strongest possible protection against external network-based attacks — appropriate when the sensitivity of the data or system genuinely justifies that trade, and a significant operational cost otherwise.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming a deployment process validated in a connected environment will work unchanged air-gapped.** As the code example shows, any step that silently reaches out to the network on demand becomes a hard blocker with no fallback in an air-gapped environment — this has to be tested air-gapped, not assumed.

**Underestimating the lead time an update requires.** Because updates can't be pulled instantly, planning an update for the same day it's needed doesn't work — the manual vetting and transfer process needs to be built into the schedule well in advance.

**Treating air-gapping as a default security posture rather than a deliberate, costly trade-off.** Air-gapping every system "to be safe" imposes real operational cost that isn't justified unless the data or system's sensitivity genuinely requires it.

questions.question: What does an air-gapped deployment fundamentally lack, compared to a typical connected system?
options: Any network connection to the outside internet at all
Any local storage capacity
Any ability to run AI models locally
Any users capable of accessing the system
questions.explanation: Air-gapping means complete isolation from external networks — the defining characteristic that shapes every other requirement in this lesson.

questions.question: Why does an air-gapped deployment require pre-staging container images and model weights, unlike a typical cloud deployment?
options: Because there's no internet connection available to pull them from a registry or download them on demand
Because air-gapped systems cannot run any containers or models at all
Because pre-staging is required by every cloud deployment as well, with no difference
Because container registries only work in air-gapped environments
questions.explanation: The complete absence of network access means every dependency that a connected system would fetch on demand must instead be transferred in through a controlled process beforehand.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `deploy_connected(required, staged)` succeed with `"status": "ready"` even though `llm_weights_7b` isn't in `staged`?
options: Because `deploy_connected` simply adds any missing dependency to `fetched_on_demand` and proceeds, modeling on-demand network fetching
Because `llm_weights_7b` isn't actually required by this deployment
Because `deploy_connected` ignores missing dependencies entirely without recording them
Because `staged` actually does contain `llm_weights_7b`
questions.explanation: `deploy_connected` treats any dependency not found in `available_locally` as something to fetch on demand — it never blocks, it just records what it fetched.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `deploy_air_gapped(required, staged)` return, and why?
options: `{"status": "ready", "fetched_on_demand": []}`, the same as the connected case
`{"status": "blocked", "missing": ["llm_weights_7b"]}`, because `llm_weights_7b` isn't in `available_locally` and there's no network fallback to fetch it
An exception, because the function has no handling for missing dependencies
`{"status": "ready", "fetched_on_demand": ["llm_weights_7b"]}`
questions.explanation: `deploy_air_gapped` computes `missing` as the deps not in `available_locally`; since that list is non-empty (`["llm_weights_7b"]`), it returns the blocked status rather than proceeding.

questions.question: What does the contrast between `deploy_connected` and `deploy_air_gapped` in the code example illustrate?
options: That both functions behave identically regardless of network assumptions
That a missing dependency is a minor, silently-resolved detail in a connected deployment but a hard blocker in an air-gapped one, since there's no network fallback
That air-gapped deployments never have any missing dependencies
That connected deployments always fail when a dependency is missing
questions.explanation: The two functions handle the exact same missing dependency completely differently — one absorbs it via network fetch, the other blocks entirely — capturing the core practical difference air-gapping introduces.

questions.question: What operational cost does air-gapping impose in exchange for its security benefit?
options: Updates and patches become a slower, deliberate, manually-vetted and transferred process rather than automatic
Air-gapping has no operational cost of any kind
Air-gapped systems automatically update faster than connected systems
Air-gapping eliminates the need for any security practices at all
questions.explanation: The isolation that protects against network-based attacks also removes the convenience of automatic, live updates, requiring a slower manual process instead.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against assuming a deployment process validated in a connected environment will work unchanged when air-gapped?
options: Because, as the code example shows, any step that silently reaches out to the network on demand becomes a hard blocker with no fallback in an air-gapped environment
Because air-gapped environments are always faster than connected ones
Because connected deployment processes are technically incompatible with any hardware
Because air-gapped systems automatically convert network calls into local calls
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section connects directly to the code example: what's an invisible network fetch in a connected environment becomes an outright blocker air-gapped, so the process needs air-gapped testing specifically.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating air-gapping as a default security posture rather than a deliberate trade-off?
options: Because air-gapping every system "to be safe" imposes real operational cost that isn't justified unless the data or system's sensitivity genuinely requires it
Because air-gapping is illegal for most organizations to implement
Because air-gapped systems are always less secure than connected ones
Because air-gapping requires no additional planning compared to a connected deployment
questions.explanation: The lesson frames air-gapping as a deliberate, costly trade-off appropriate only when genuinely justified — applying it by default wastes the operational convenience a connected system offers without a matching security need.

lessons.title: Private Model Hosting
lessons.description: Running the model yourself, when sending data to a third-party API isn't an option.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why an enterprise might choose **private model hosting** over a hosted LLM API, and what that choice actually requires.

sections.title: 🔒 Why not just use a hosted API
sections.content: The LLM Engineering course's default assumption was often calling a hosted LLM API — simple, fast to start, no infrastructure to manage. For an enterprise handling sensitive data, sending that data to a third-party API may be contractually prohibited, legally restricted, or simply an unacceptable risk regardless of the provider's own security claims — private hosting keeps data and inference entirely within infrastructure the organization controls.

sections.title: 🏗️ What private hosting actually requires
sections.content: This means directly applying the Inference course's entire toolkit — serving frameworks like vLLM, GPU infrastructure from the Cloud course, quantization and batching for cost-effective serving — as an in-house operational responsibility rather than something abstracted away behind an API call. The convenience of "just call the API" is traded for full ownership of the serving stack.

sections.title: ⚖️ Open-weight models make this practical
sections.content: Private hosting depends on having a model you're actually allowed to run yourself — **open-weight models** (covered in the Hugging Face course) make this practical in a way that a closed, API-only model does not, since there's no weights to host privately for a model you can only access through someone else's hosted endpoint.

sections.title: 💰 The cost trade-off is real, not automatic savings
sections.content: Private hosting isn't automatically cheaper than a hosted API — it trades a per-token API cost for the fixed and ongoing costs of GPU infrastructure, serving engineering, and operational overhead, which only pays off at sufficient volume or when the data-control requirement makes the hosted API option unavailable regardless of cost.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a simplified simulation comparing hosted-API cost against private-hosting cost across different usage volumes:

```python
def hosted_api_monthly_cost(tokens_per_month, price_per_million_tokens):
    return (tokens_per_month / 1_000_000) * price_per_million_tokens

def private_hosting_monthly_cost(fixed_gpu_cost, ops_engineering_cost):
    return fixed_gpu_cost + ops_engineering_cost  # roughly volume-independent within capacity

price_per_million = 15.0
fixed_gpu_cost = 12000
ops_cost = 8000

for tokens in [5_000_000, 500_000_000, 2_000_000_000]:
    hosted = hosted_api_monthly_cost(tokens, price_per_million)
    private = private_hosting_monthly_cost(fixed_gpu_cost, ops_cost)
    cheaper = "hosted API" if hosted < private else "private hosting"
    print(f"{tokens:,} tokens/mo -> hosted: ${hosted:,.2f}, private: ${private:,.2f} -> cheaper: {cheaper}")
```

At 5,000,000 tokens/month, `hosted = (5_000_000/1_000_000) * 15.0 = 75.0`, far below the fixed private cost of `12000 + 8000 = 20000` — the hosted API is dramatically cheaper at low volume. At 500,000,000 tokens/month, `hosted = 500 * 15.0 = 7500.0`, still below the flat `20000` private cost. Only at 2,000,000,000 tokens/month does `hosted = 2000 * 15.0 = 30000.0` exceed the private hosting's flat `20000` — private hosting only becomes cheaper once volume is high enough to amortize its fixed costs, exactly the volume-dependence the lesson describes; below that crossover, "private is more secure" and "private is cheaper" are two entirely separate claims.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming private hosting is automatically cheaper than a hosted API.** As the code example shows, private hosting's cost is only justified by volume above a real crossover point — below it, a hosted API is simply less expensive, and the decision to self-host should rest on data-control needs or confirmed volume economics, not an assumption.

**Choosing private hosting without an open-weight model actually available.** Private hosting requires having weights to host — committing to a private-hosting architecture before confirming an appropriate open-weight model exists for the use case puts the plan on an unverified foundation.

**Underestimating the ongoing operational engineering cost, not just the GPU bill.** The serving stack — batching, quantization, scaling, monitoring — is real, ongoing engineering work, not a one-time setup cost that disappears after initial deployment.

questions.question: Why might an enterprise choose private model hosting over a hosted LLM API, despite the added operational burden?
options: Because sending sensitive data to a third-party API may be contractually prohibited, legally restricted, or an unacceptable risk regardless of cost
Because private hosting is always cheaper than any hosted API option
Because hosted APIs cannot process any enterprise data under any circumstances
Because private hosting requires no infrastructure investment at all
questions.explanation: Data-control requirements — legal, contractual, or risk-based — are often the deciding factor, independent of whether private hosting is cheaper.

questions.question: What does private model hosting require that using a hosted API does not?
options: Directly operating the Inference course's serving stack — frameworks, GPU infrastructure, quantization — as an in-house responsibility
Nothing additional; the requirements are identical to using a hosted API
The complete absence of any GPU hardware
A guarantee of automatic cost savings regardless of usage volume
questions.explanation: Private hosting means taking on the full serving-infrastructure responsibility that a hosted API would otherwise abstract away behind a simple API call.

questions.question: In the code example, at 5,000,000 tokens/month, why is the hosted API cheaper than private hosting?
options: Because `hosted_api_monthly_cost` returns `75.0`, far below the flat `private_hosting_monthly_cost` of `20000`, since the fixed GPU and ops costs aren't amortized over enough volume yet
Because private hosting has no cost at low volume
Because the hosted API's price scales down to zero below a certain volume
Because 5,000,000 tokens exceeds the private hosting capacity
questions.explanation: `(5_000_000/1_000_000) * 15.0 = 75.0`, dramatically below the volume-independent `12000 + 8000 = 20000` private cost — at this volume the fixed private infrastructure costs simply aren't worth it yet.

questions.question: In the code example, at what volume does private hosting first become cheaper than the hosted API, and why?
options: At 500,000,000 tokens/month, because hosted cost already exceeds 20000 there

At 2,000,000,000 tokens/month, because `hosted_api_monthly_cost` there is `30000.0`, which exceeds the flat private cost of `20000`, while at 500,000,000 tokens the hosted cost (`7500.0`) is still below it
Private hosting is never cheaper in this example
At 5,000,000 tokens/month, the lowest volume shown
questions.explanation: At 500,000,000 tokens, hosted cost is `7500.0` (still cheaper than 20000); only at 2,000,000,000 tokens does hosted cost reach `30000.0`, crossing above the flat `20000` private cost.

questions.question: What does the code example demonstrate about the relationship between usage volume and which option is cheaper?
options: That private hosting is always cheaper regardless of volume
That the hosted API's cost scales with volume while private hosting's cost stays roughly flat, so which option is cheaper depends on where volume falls relative to a crossover point
That the hosted API is always cheaper regardless of volume
That volume has no bearing on which option is more cost-effective
questions.explanation: The three printed comparisons show the hosted API's linear scaling crossing above private hosting's flat cost only at high volume — the crossover point is exactly what determines which is cheaper.

questions.question: Why do open-weight models matter specifically for private hosting?
options: Because private hosting requires actually having and running the model's weights yourself, which only open-weight models make possible
Because open-weight models cannot be hosted privately under any circumstances
Because closed, API-only models are always better suited to private hosting
Because open-weight models require no GPU infrastructure at all
questions.explanation: A model only accessible through someone else's hosted API has no weights available to host privately — open-weight availability is a precondition for this deployment choice.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against assuming private hosting is automatically cheaper than a hosted API?
options: Because, as the code example shows, private hosting's cost is only justified by volume above a real crossover point — below it, a hosted API is simply less expensive
Because private hosting is illegal below a certain volume threshold
Because hosted APIs always cost more than private hosting at every volume
Because private hosting has no fixed costs at all
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section states this directly, and the code example shows the concrete crossover point below which the assumption of automatic savings is simply wrong.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against underestimating the ongoing operational engineering cost of private hosting, not just the GPU bill?
options: Because batching, quantization, scaling, and monitoring are real, ongoing engineering work, not a one-time setup cost that disappears after initial deployment
Because operational engineering cost is always zero for private hosting
Because the GPU bill is the only cost that ever matters for private hosting
Because ongoing engineering work is only needed for hosted APIs, not private hosting
questions.explanation: The code example's `ops_engineering_cost` term captures exactly this — a persistent monthly cost alongside the GPU cost, reflecting that the serving stack needs continuous engineering attention.

lessons.title: Choosing a Deployment Model
lessons.description: Bringing this module's three deployment options together into one concrete decision framework.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Apply a structured decision process for choosing among on-prem, cloud, hybrid, air-gapped, and privately-hosted deployment for a given enterprise AI use case.

sections.title: ❓ The questions that actually drive this decision
sections.content:
- What does data sensitivity and regulation actually **require**, not just prefer?
- What's the actual traffic volume and its variability, which affects whether cloud elasticity or fixed on-prem capacity fits better?
- What operational capacity does the organization have to run infrastructure itself, echoing the Vector Databases course's managed-vs-self-hosted framework?
- Is any part of this workload's data or process legally required to stay within a specific jurisdiction or off any external network entirely?

sections.title: 🧮 A worked example
sections.content: A healthcare enterprise building a clinical documentation assistant: patient data likely has strict regulatory requirements (HIPAA-adjacent, covered more in the governance module), pointing toward private hosting or a tightly controlled hybrid model — a public hosted API handling that data directly would likely be a non-starter regardless of the API's own security posture, not because the security is inadequate but because the compliance requirement is categorical rather than a risk-tolerance judgment call.

sections.title: 🚪 Not a permanent, unchangeable decision
sections.content: As covered for narrower infrastructure choices earlier in this curriculum (the Vector Databases course's migration lesson, the App Dev course's monolith-to-microservices lesson), a deployment model chosen today can be revisited as requirements, regulations, or the organization's own capabilities change — but each of these deployment models involves enough infrastructure investment that changing course is a real, planned undertaking, not a quick config change.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Letting general preference or trend override what data sensitivity and regulation actually require.** As the worked example shows, some requirements are categorical — no amount of preference for a simpler architecture changes what's actually permitted.

**Treating this decision as a one-time, unchangeable commitment.** Failing to revisit the deployment model as requirements evolve can leave a system stuck on an architecture that no longer fits its actual needs.

**Treating this decision as trivially reversible.** The opposite mistake is just as costly — underestimating the real infrastructure investment involved means a change of course gets attempted as a quick fix rather than the planned undertaking it actually requires.

questions.question: What should primarily drive the choice between on-prem, cloud, hybrid, air-gapped, or privately-hosted deployment?
options: Actual data sensitivity/regulatory requirements, traffic patterns, and organizational operational capacity — not general preference
Whichever option is most popular among other companies
Always the cheapest option available regardless of any other factor
Always the option requiring the least amount of initial paperwork
questions.explanation: Concrete requirements — regulatory, operational, and traffic-based — should drive this decision, the same requirements-first discipline used for infrastructure choices throughout this curriculum.

questions.question: For a healthcare clinical documentation assistant handling patient data, why might a public hosted API be a non-starter regardless of its security quality?
options: Because the compliance requirement for that kind of data may be categorical, not a risk-tolerance judgment that a good security posture alone can satisfy
Because hosted APIs are always technically incapable of processing healthcare data
Because on-premises deployment is illegal for healthcare organizations
Because clinical documentation assistants never need any deployment decision
questions.explanation: Some regulatory requirements aren't about how good a third party's security is — they categorically restrict where certain data types may go, regardless of the provider's actual practices.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `recommend_deployment(clinical_assistant)` return "private hosting or tightly controlled hybrid" regardless of `traffic_variability` and `ops_capacity`?
options: Because `regulatory_category == "categorical"` matches the second `if` branch, which returns immediately without evaluating the traffic or ops-capacity conditions that come after it
Because `traffic_variability` is set to `"high"` for this workload
Because `jurisdiction_locked` is `True` for the clinical assistant
Because the function ignores `regulatory_category` entirely
questions.explanation: The function checks `jurisdiction_locked` first (False, skipped), then `regulatory_category == "categorical"` (True), returning immediately — the third branch checking traffic and ops capacity is never reached.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `recommend_deployment(marketing_tool)` return "cloud"?
options: Because `jurisdiction_locked` is `False` and `regulatory_category` is `"none"`, so both earlier branches are skipped, and `traffic_variability == "high" and ops_capacity == "low"` matches the third branch
Because marketing tools are hardcoded to always return "cloud"
Because `regulatory_category` is `"categorical"` for the marketing tool
Because the function defaults to "cloud" when no answers dict is provided
questions.explanation: With no jurisdiction lock and a non-categorical regulatory category, execution reaches the third branch, where `traffic_variability="high"` and `ops_capacity="low"` together match, returning "cloud".

questions.question: What does the ordering of checks in `recommend_deployment` illustrate about how the decision framework should be applied?
options: That jurisdiction and categorical regulatory requirements should be checked first, since they override traffic and operational-capacity considerations entirely when present
That traffic variability is always the most important factor to check first
That all four conditions must be true simultaneously for any recommendation to be made
That the order of checks has no effect on the final recommendation
questions.explanation: The function's structure — jurisdiction first, then categorical regulation, then traffic/ops — reflects that hard legal constraints should short-circuit the decision before softer operational trade-offs are even considered.

questions.question: Why is a deployment model decision described as 'not permanent' but also not something to change lightly?
options: Because it can be revisited as requirements change, but the infrastructure investment involved makes changing course a real, planned undertaking rather than a quick fix
Because deployment models can be changed instantly with a single configuration flag
Because deployment models, once chosen, can genuinely never be changed under any circumstances
Because this decision has no infrastructure implications worth planning around
questions.explanation: Like other infrastructure decisions covered earlier in this curriculum, this one remains revisitable in principle but carries enough real investment that changing it deserves deliberate planning, not casual reversal.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against letting general preference override what data sensitivity and regulation actually require?
options: Because, as the worked example shows, some requirements are categorical — no amount of preference for a simpler architecture changes what's actually legally permitted
Because preference should always be the primary factor in deployment decisions
Because regulatory requirements never actually constrain deployment choice in practice
Because data sensitivity has no bearing on deployment architecture
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section reinforces the worked example's point directly — categorical requirements aren't a preference to be weighed against convenience, they're a hard constraint.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating a deployment model change as trivially reversible?
options: Because underestimating the real infrastructure investment involved means a change of course gets attempted as a quick fix rather than the planned undertaking it actually requires
Because deployment models can never be changed under any circumstances
Because reversibility has no bearing on how a deployment change should be planned
Because infrastructure investment is irrelevant to deployment model changes
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section flags this as the opposite failure mode from treating the decision as permanent — underestimating the real cost of change leads to rushed, under-planned migrations.
